content: Congenital syphilis is becoming an increasingly significant public health issue, particularly in many developing nations and in the transitional economies of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. This rise in cases has been further exacerbated in some regions by the concurrent HIV/AIDS epidemic. Although the efficacy of penicillin in treating syphilis during pregnancy and preventing congenital syphilis was established shortly after its introduction in the 1940s, there remains considerable uncertainty regarding the most effective treatment regimens for this condition. The primary objective of this review was to determine the most effective antibiotic treatment regimen for syphilis in pregnant women, both with and without coexisting HIV infection. This includes identifying the optimal dose, duration of treatment, and mode of administration. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched as of December 2009 to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria specified that any trial attempting to allocate treatment for syphilis during pregnancy using a random or quasi-random method would be considered for review. Data extraction was performed using a standardized data collection sheet. The extracted information included the entry criteria for participants, the source of control groups, and whether the authors of the studies stratified their findings based on the stage of pregnancy at which syphilis was diagnosed. A total of 29 studies were identified as meeting the criteria for detailed evaluation. However, none of these studies satisfied the pre-determined criteria for comparative groups, and none included comparisons between groups of pregnant women who were randomly allocated to different treatment regimens. The authors concluded that while penicillin is unequivocally effective in treating syphilis during pregnancy and preventing congenital syphilis, there is still uncertainty regarding the optimal treatment regimens. Further research is necessary to investigate cases of treatment failure with currently recommended regimens. Such studies should also assess the potential impact of HIV infection on the effectiveness of prenatal syphilis treatment. Randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy of various antibiotic regimens for treating primary and secondary syphilis in pregnant women. These trials should include comparisons with existing treatment recommendations and explore the use of oral antibiotics, which may be particularly relevant in resource-limited settings where access to safe needles and syringes cannot be guaranteed.
